scope: Source-backed reconstruction of Orion European Service Module propulsion architecture and the public evidence boundary for selecting propulsion hardware for Artemis II trajectory correction burns.

sources.title: European Service Module: Propulsion
claims_used: The European Service Module propulsion system contains 33 engines of three types.
The main engine provides 25.7 kN and is gimballed in pitch and yaw.
Eight fixed R-4D-11 auxiliary engines provide 490 N each.
The auxiliary engines provide orbit corrections and backup capability for the main engine.
Twenty-four 220 N reaction-control engines are arranged in six pods of four.
The reaction-control engines provide attitude control.

sources.title: European Service Module engines powering Artemis II
claims_used: Artemis II carries 33 European Service Module engines.
One main engine provides large velocity changes.
Eight auxiliary engines support orbital corrections and can back up the main engine.
Twenty-four reaction-control engines are arranged in six pods and provide precise rotational and orientation control.
The reaction-control system engines are used during the Artemis II proximity-operations demonstration.
The European Service Module main engine performs Artemis II translunar injection.

sources.title: How to go to the Moon
claims_used: Artemis II translunar injection uses the European Service Module main engine.
Trajectory correction maneuvers use the European Service Module's smaller engines.
Flight rules determine which engine class is used for a trajectory correction.
Auxiliary engines are available for larger adjustments and as backup for the main engine.
Reaction-control thrusters are available for finer corrections.
A brief reaction-control firing of around ten seconds was given as an example of a slight correction.

sources.title: Artemis II Press Kit
claims_used: NASA's premission plan described three smaller outbound trajectory correction burns as using Orion's orbital maneuvering system engine.
The translunar injection was planned for Orion's main engine.
Three return trajectory correction burns were planned on the trans-Earth leg.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Update: Perigee Raise Burn Complete
claims_used: Orion ignited the service module main engine for 43 seconds for the perigee raise burn.

sources.title: Artemis II: splashdown
claims_used: The Artemis II translunar injection was a 350-second burn performed by the European Service Module main engine.
The translunar injection was sufficiently precise that two of the three planned outbound trajectory corrections were cancelled.
Three trajectory correction burns occurred during the return to Earth.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 5: Correction Burn Complete
claims_used: The executed outbound correction began at 11:03 p.m. EDT and lasted 17.5 seconds.
The report does not identify a specific propulsion engine class.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 7: First Return Correction Burn Complete
claims_used: RTC1 ignited Orion's thrusters for 15 seconds.
RTC1 produced a reported velocity change of 1.6 feet per second.
The report does not identify the propulsion engine class.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 9: Second Return Correction Burn Complete
claims_used: RTC2 ignited Orion's thrusters for nine seconds.
RTC2 produced a reported velocity change of 5.3 feet per second.
The report does not identify the propulsion engine class.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 10: Crew Completes Final Burn Before Splashdown
claims_used: RTC3 ignited Orion's thrusters for eight seconds.
RTC3 produced a reported velocity change of 4.2 feet per second.
The report does not identify the propulsion engine class.

source_relationship.interpretation: The NASA premission plan and ESA operational explanation are preserved as distinct evidence layers. They may reflect different planning assumptions, scope, or evolving operational practice. Without burn-specific as-flown identification, MissionLab does not select one claim as the executed engine assignment.

guardrails: European Service Module propulsion architecture describes capability and does not by itself establish burn-specific as-flown engine selection.
The NASA premission outbound-correction OMS-E plan is not treated as burn-specific as-flown evidence.
The ESA flight-rule explanation is not treated as a burn-specific assignment record.
The NASA and ESA correction-engine descriptions are preserved as separate evidence layers rather than silently reconciled.
The phrase 'ignited its thrusters' does not identify the auxiliary engine class.
The phrase 'ignited its thrusters' does not identify the reaction-control engine class.
OTC3 lacking explicit engine-class wording does not permit an inferred engine assignment.
Burn duration alone does not establish engine class.
Reported delta-v magnitude alone does not establish engine class.
Per-engine nominal thrust ratios are architecture comparisons only and are not spacecraft acceleration ratios.
Twenty-four RCS engines multiplied by 220 N must not be interpreted as simultaneously available one-direction thrust.
No burn-specific impulse is computed from nominal thrust and duration when the as-flown engine assignment is unresolved.
Perigee raise and translunar injection are retained as confirmed main-engine examples and must not be generalized automatically to the smaller trajectory corrections.
